title: Electromagnetic induction
target: Explain why changing magnetic flux can induce an emf.
criteria: Identify a change in magnetic flux.
Predict whether a stationary arrangement produces sustained induction.
Use Lenz’s law to describe opposition to change.

authoring.limitations: Reasoning evidence only. Multiple choice does not certify physical performance. Teacher reviews before assigning and rates mastery separately.

cpa.prompt: A coil is rotated in a steady uniform magnetic field so that the flux through it changes. Can an emf be induced?
options: No; a coil must touch the magnet.
No; only a changing field magnitude can induce emf.
Yes; changing orientation can change flux even when field magnitude is steady.
Yes, but only if magnetic poles are electrically charged.
cpa.guide: Flux depends on field, area, and orientation. Its rate of change determines induced emf.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Compare evidence and identify a physical relationship.

cpa.prompt: A fixed coil’s area and orientation stay constant while the perpendicular magnetic field grows. What quantity changes?
options: Only its color.
Magnetic flux through the coil.
The coil must lose all resistance.
The definition of charge.
cpa.guide: Flux through a fixed area changes when its perpendicular magnetic field changes.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

cpa.prompt: A magnet and coil are fixed relative to each other. Their field, area, and orientation are constant. What sustained emf does Faraday’s law predict from this arrangement?
options: A steadily increasing emf.
Zero.
A nonzero emf solely because a magnet exists.
An emf equal to the magnet’s mass.
cpa.guide: Faraday emf requires changing flux, not simply nonzero flux.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A magnet is moved into a coil, then held still. What should happen to the motion-induced emf after it is held still?
options: It doubles because the magnet is nearer.
It keeps the peak moving value forever.
It grows forever.
It becomes zero once flux stops changing.
cpa.guide: Holding it stationary removes the flux change after motion stops.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A north pole approaches a conducting loop. By Lenz’s law, the induced magnetic effect tends to…
options: oppose the increase in magnetic flux caused by the approach.
destroy the approaching magnet.
increase the change without any energy input.
eliminate all magnetic field everywhere.
cpa.guide: The induced effect opposes the flux change, not necessarily the field itself.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

cpa.prompt: A magnet withdraws from a coil after previously approaching it along the same path. Which qualitative comparison follows?
options: The coil produces emf only during approach.
The sign must stay the same because the pole is unchanged.
The induced emf reverses sign when the flux-change direction reverses.
The coil acquires a permanent battery voltage.
cpa.guide: Approach and withdrawal produce opposite flux-change signs; the emf sign reverses.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Compare evidence and identify a physical relationship.
